title: Two hundred applications and not one licensed
excerpt: General recruitment portals fail when employers need verified technical licenses, opening a clear path for small operators to build specialized job boards.
html:
A hiring manager at a commercial electrical shop opens his inbox at seven in the morning. He posted an opening for a Class-1 Licensed Wireman three days ago on a large general job portal. He spent fifty thousand rupees on the sponsored listing. The site sent him two hundred and fourteen applications. He opens the first twenty PDFs. Every single applicant holds a basic high school diploma or a general computer training certificate. Not one has a state electrical license. He selects all two hundred and fourteen files and drags them into the trash bin. He has wasted three hours and still has an empty work site.

That manager does not need more applications. He needs three resumes from people who can legally touch a high-voltage panel. This mess happens thousands of times a day across blue-collar and technical industries. General job boards collect fees by maximizing the total volume of clicks and uploads. They do not care if an applicant is legally qualified to step onto a factory floor. If you want to understand how to start a niche job board that actually makes money, this exact frustration is your starting point.

The reason general platforms fail certified trades

Big job sites are built for generic office work. Their search filters look for keywords like management, communication, or spreadsheets. They do not know how to handle trade certification screening. A state wireman license, a certified boiler operator permit, or an AWS pipe welding ticket is not just a keyword on a resume. It is a legal document issued by a government board with a registration number and an expiration date.

When an industrial plant needs a boiler engineer, hiring someone without a valid permit can close the factory down during a state inspection. If they post the opening on a massive general site, thousands of underqualified job seekers submit their resumes with one click. The employer receives a flood of useless noise. They have to assign an assistant to call dozens of applicants just to ask for their license numbers.

A specialized board solves this by changing the entry rules. Instead of asking candidates for a standard CV, your platform forces them to enter their trade license number, state issuing authority, and expiration year before they can submit an application. You do not need complex software to do this. A basic web form with mandatory text fields achieves what a multi-billion-dollar platform fails to do.

The job board cold start problem on zero budget

Every two-sided marketplace faces the same wall when it starts. Employers will not pay to post open roles if there are no qualified candidates searching the site. Candidates will not waste time setting up profiles if there are no open jobs listed. This chicken-and-egg dynamic is the job board cold start problem. It stops most founders before they land a single paying customer.

If you have money, you spend it on digital ads to acquire both sides at the same time. If you are starting with zero capital, you cannot buy traffic. You must build your platform manually by acting as the relay between both parties before you ever write a line of software or charge a fee.

Start by hunting for open jobs that are already public. Search local newspaper classifieds, regional trade association notice boards, and direct company career pages in your chosen industry. Find ten employers currently looking for licensed workers. Do not steal their job ads or scrape their sites automatically. Call the owner or the head of maintenance directly on the phone.

Tell them you run a dedicated board specifically for certified tradespeople in their sector. Ask for permission to re-post their open position on your board for free. Tell them plainly that you will personally verify the license details of every candidate before forwarding their profile. Nine out of ten managers will give you permission because it costs them nothing and saves them from digging through junk emails.

Achieving marketplace liquidity in a tiny niche

Marketplace liquidity does not mean having one hundred thousand registered users. It means that when an employer posts an open job on your site, they get at least three fully qualified, available candidates within seventy-two hours. If you achieve that match rate consistently, employers will pay you every month regardless of how small your total candidate database is.

To build this density without spending on marketing, pick one narrow trade and one specific industrial district. Do not launch a general trade job board for all of India or even all of Maharashtra. Launch a job site exclusively for certified industrial electricians in the Thane-Belapur industrial belt. Narrowing your focus makes finding candidates manageable through targeted outreach.

Go to the places where these tradespeople hang out online and offline. Search for regional Telegram groups, WhatsApp communities, and Facebook forums dedicated to local industrial workers. Do not spam them with links to a blank website. Share useful industry news, state licensing exam updates, or wage discussions. When you have a verified, open job from a local contractor, post the job details directly into the group with a direct contact link.

Your goal for the first two months is simple. You want to personally talk to twenty licensed workers every week. Write down their license numbers, current employment status, expected daily wages, and preferred shifts in a plain spreadsheet. Once you have fifty verified candidates in one city, you have built real liquidity for that single trade.

Manual trade certification screening as your core service

Software automation is useful later, but manual effort is how you win your first paying customers. Big job boards cannot afford to have a human check every application. You can. That manual effort is your advantage over a multi-million-dollar competitor.

When a candidate submits their details to your board, perform the trade certification screening yourself before the employer ever sees the file. Go to the state government licensing board website and type in the license number. Check if the candidate's full name matches the state database record. Verify that the permit is current and has not been suspended for safety violations.

Next, place a quick phone call to the applicant. Keep it under three minutes. Ask three direct questions:

  • What is your exact license or certification number?
  • Are you currently employed, and how many days of notice do you need to start a new role?
  • Are you willing to work night shifts at the standard local industrial rate?

If they answer clearly and their license is valid in the government registry, move their profile to the employer's dashboard or email it directly to the hiring manager with a red checkmark badge next to their name. When a hiring manager receives three resumes that are all pre-screened and legally ready to work, you have saved them five hours of admin work. That is when a free customer turns into a paying customer.

Turning manual matches into a repeatable business model

Do not charge employers until you have proven you can send them pre-screened candidates. Trying to charge five thousand rupees for a job post on a brand-new, empty website is the fastest way to fail. Run your first five employer placements completely free of charge.

Once you send an employer two verified candidates who pass their technical interview, send a plain invoice for the next job listing. You can charge a flat fee per job post or a fee for every verified candidate intro you provide. For deep dive calculations on pricing structures, platform mechanics, and technical trade verticals, read the full trade job board blueprint.

Keep your operating expenses as close to zero as possible. You do not need a custom mobile app or an expensive enterprise website template. A free WordPress setup with a basic directory plugin, or even a simple NoCode web page paired with a Google Form, is enough to run this business for the first six months. Spend your time on the phone with candidates and shop managers, not tweaking website fonts.

As candidate volume grows, you will spend most of your mornings verifying licenses on state portals and your afternoons calling hiring managers. Once you reach thirty active employer accounts in one sector, you can hire a junior recruiter to handle the phone verification calls while you expand the service into a second industrial city.

What to do this week

You can test this concept in seven days without spending money or registering a company. Follow these three steps to make your first move:

  1. Pick one licensed trade in your local industrial area. Choose a role that legally requires a state ticket or safety permit, such as a Class-1 wireman, commercial refrigeration mechanic, or certified crane operator.
  2. Call five local contractors or maintenance managers. Ask them how many hours they spent deleting bad applications during their last hiring round. Ask if they will let you send them three pre-screened, verified candidates for their next open role for free.
  3. Build a simple candidate intake form. Create a free online form that makes license numbers, state issuing bodies, and license expiration dates mandatory fields before a candidate can apply.
